title: EXCEPT
description: EXCEPT returns the rows in the first result set that do NOT appear in the second. Write a query that returns the `customer_id` of every customer who has placed at least one order but has NEVER had an appointment.
hints: Putting EXCEPT between "customer_id from orders" and "customer_id from appointments" keeps only the ids from the FIRST query that are missing from the second - order matters here, unlike UNION or INTERSECT.
Select customer_id from orders, put EXCEPT between the two queries, then select customer_id from appointments - orders has to come first.
expected_behavior: Returns the distinct customer_id values that appear in orders but not in appointments.
solution: SELECT customer_id FROM orders EXCEPT SELECT customer_id FROM appointments;
explanation: EXCEPT is set subtraction - "everything in A that isn't also in B." Swapping the two sides gives a completely different (and usually different-sized) result, so the order you write them in matters.
postgres_note: Some other databases (MySQL historically, for one) spell this MINUS instead of EXCEPT - Postgres follows the SQL standard name, EXCEPT.
